```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3, fig.align = "center")
library(ggplot2); data(ToothGrowth)
tg <- ToothGrowth; tg$dose <- factor(tg$dose)
```

## Data and exploratory analysis

`ToothGrowth` records tooth length (`len`) of 60 guinea pigs given vitamin C at three doses
(0.5, 1, 2 mg/day) by orange juice (OJ) or ascorbic acid (VC); 10 animals per supp-dose cell.

```{r summ}
agg <- aggregate(len ~ supp + dose, tg, function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
knitr::kable(do.call(data.frame, agg), digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Supp", "Dose", "n", "Mean len", "SD"))
```

```{r box, fig.cap="Figure 1: Tooth length by dose and supplement."}
ggplot(tg, aes(dose, len, fill = supp)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length", fill = "Supplement") + theme_minimal()
```

Length rises clearly with dose for both supplements. OJ appears higher at 0.5 and 1 mg, while at 2 mg the two look similar.

## Comparisons

I use two-sample t confidence intervals / tests (unequal variances, Welch, the default of
`t.test`), 95% level. Supplement comparisons are unpaired (different animals).

```{r tests}
res <- function(x, y, paired = FALSE) {
  t <- t.test(x, y, paired = paired)
  c(diff = unname(t$estimate[1] - t$estimate[2]), lo = t$conf.int[1], hi = t$conf.int[2], p = t$p.value)
}
L <- function(s, d) tg$len[tg$supp == s & tg$dose == d]
rows <- list(
  "OJ vs VC, all doses" = res(tg$len[tg$supp=="OJ"], tg$len[tg$supp=="VC"]),
  "OJ vs VC, dose 0.5"  = res(L("OJ","0.5"), L("VC","0.5")),
  "OJ vs VC, dose 1"    = res(L("OJ","1"),   L("VC","1")),
  "OJ vs VC, dose 2"    = res(L("OJ","2"),   L("VC","2")),
  "Dose 1 vs 0.5 (all supp)" = res(tg$len[tg$dose=="1"], tg$len[tg$dose=="0.5"]),
  "Dose 2 vs 1 (all supp)"   = res(tg$len[tg$dose=="2"], tg$len[tg$dose=="1"]),
  "Dose 2 vs 0.5 (all supp)" = res(tg$len[tg$dose=="2"], tg$len[tg$dose=="0.5"]))
tab <- do.call(rbind, rows)
tab <- data.frame(Comparison = rownames(tab), round(tab, 3), row.names = NULL)
tab$p <- ifelse(tab$p < 0.001, "<0.001", format(round(tab$p, 3), nsmall = 3))
knitr::kable(tab, col.names = c("Comparison", "Mean diff", "CI low", "CI high", "p-value"))
```

## Conclusions

* **Dose:** each increase in dose raises mean tooth length significantly; all three dose
  comparisons have CIs entirely above 0 and p < 0.001. Doubling from 0.5 to 2 mg adds about 15 units.
* **Supplement, overall:** OJ is higher by about 3.7 units, but the CI (about $-0.17$ to $7.57$) includes 0 (p ≈ 0.06),
  so pooled across doses we cannot conclude a difference at the 5% level.
* **Supplement within dose:** OJ gives significantly longer teeth at 0.5 mg (p ≈ 0.006) and 1 mg (p ≈ 0.001); at 2 mg
  there is no evidence of a difference (CI includes 0, p ≈ 0.96). So the OJ advantage appears at lower doses and vanishes at the highest.

**Assumptions.** Animals are independent and randomly assigned to supplement/dose; lengths are approximately
normal within groups (or samples large enough for the t approximation, a limitation with n = 10 per cell);
variances may differ (hence Welch). Comparisons are not corrected for multiple testing (7 tests), so results
should be read cautiously. The dose effects and the OJ effects at 0.5 mg (p ≈ 0.006) and 1 mg survive a Bonferroni
threshold of 0.05/7 ≈ 0.007, though 0.5 mg only just.

## Appendix: code

```{r app, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
data(ToothGrowth); tg <- ToothGrowth; tg$dose <- factor(tg$dose)
t.test(len ~ supp, data = tg)                                  # pooled over dose
t.test(len ~ supp, data = subset(tg, dose == 0.5))             # per dose
t.test(tg$len[tg$dose==1], tg$len[tg$dose==0.5])               # dose contrasts
```
